headline: Investors Flee Stocks for Bonds, Easing Rates
tileReason: A sharp stock sell-off sent money into bonds, pulling Treasury yields to a three-week low even though wholesale inflation ran hot.
takeaway: Yesterday's inflation scare faded: the daily 30-year average closed at 7.45%, basically unchanged, and Freddie Mac's weekly average held at 7.40%. This morning bonds rallied hard as investors pulled money out of tech stocks, so lenders may price a bit lower today even though wholesale inflation came in hot. Over the next month, lower rates look slightly more likely than higher ones, but nothing is certain.

drivers.title: Investors fled stocks for bonds
drivers.text: A sell-off in AI and tech stocks spread overseas, with South Korea's market falling about 8% and triggering a trading halt. Investors moved money into U.S. Treasury bonds as a safe place to wait. More buying pushes bond prices up and yields down, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell about 0.13% to roughly 5.05%, a three-week low. Mortgage rates tend to follow that yield.

drivers.title: Fed officials signaled patience
drivers.text: Fed Governor Michelle Bowman said the Fed has time to wait after its September hike, and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said another hike is likely but not urgent. Traders cut the odds of an October 28 hike from about 54% after Wednesday's inflation report to about 30%. Fewer expected hikes take some upward pressure off longer-term rates.

drivers.title: Wholesale inflation surged
drivers.text: The producer price index (PPI), which tracks prices businesses pay, jumped 1.3% in September versus a 0.5% forecast and is up 6.3% from a year ago. Core PPI, which leaves out food and energy, rose 0.7% against a 0.3% forecast. Today the stock sell-off overshadowed it, but costs like these can reach consumers later, which is why markets still see a Fed hike by December as close to certain.

drivers.title: Shoppers kept spending
drivers.text: Retail sales rose 0.8% in September, well above the 0.3% forecast, and new jobless claims stayed low at 199,000. A strong consumer gives the Fed less reason to hold off on hikes, which leans against lower rates.

drivers.title: Oil prices slipped
drivers.text: Crude fell about 2% on reports that Washington may ease sanctions on some oil tankers, leaving Brent near $104 a barrel. Cheaper energy eases inflation worries a little, which helps rates.

outlook.basis: I now lean slightly toward lower rates. This morning's bond rally has the 10-year about 0.14% below where it stood when the 7.45% reading was set, and Fed officials are signaling they are in no hurry to hike in October. What keeps me from leaning further: wholesale inflation was very hot, a December hike is still almost fully priced in, and rallies driven by stock-market fear can reverse quickly once markets calm down. The gap between mortgage rates and the 10-year is also still wider than normal (about 2.19% vs. a typical 2.00%).
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: Rates have held around 7.4% to 7.5% for two weeks, and this morning's bond rally may bring small improvements in lender pricing. With the Fed meeting on October 28 and inflation still hot, it's worth asking your lender how a lock, a float-down option, or a short wait would each work for your timeline.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates around 7.4% are still stretching buyers' budgets. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to buy down their rate, can help your home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Rates are steady near 7.4%, and a rush into bonds this morning could nudge them a little lower, but the Fed's October 28 decision is the next big test.
